thread.title: De-Fanged: Why Megacaps Underperform - iShares S&P 100 ETF (NYSEARCA:OEF)

author: Ploutos
title: De-Fanged: Why Megacaps Underperform - iShares S&P 100 ETF (NYSEARCA:OEF)
text:
Since the S&P 500 ( SPY ) hit its market high on September 20th, the broad market gauge has sold off by 10%. The FANG stocks - Facebook ( FB ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Netflix ( NFLX ), and the artist formerly known as Google ( GOOGL ) - and their compatriot Apple ( AAPL ) have garnered headlines by appreciably underperforming the broader market as detailed below. Alphabet is the outperformer down just 13.5% with the other four megacap stocks down roughly 20% or more.
Source: Bloomberg
Before you look to buy the dip on the FANG stocks given their tendency to strongly outperform in the post-crisis era, remember that mega caps do not tend to outperform ad infinitum. Apple (#1 by market capitalization), Amazon (#3), Alphabet (#4), Facebook (#7), and Netflix (#41) are among the dominating megacaps that have powered stocks higher in recent years.
Over long time intervals, the largest S&P 500 constituents tend to underperform the broader market. Below I have graphed the S&P 100 (NYSEARCA: OEF ), the 100 largest constituents of the S&P 500, versus the broader benchmark over a period dating back to the bicentennial.
Source: Bloomberg
Over this long time interval, the S&P 500 (orange) has outperformed the S&P 100 (white) meaningfully. If you had owned the 100 largest companies in the S&P 500 by market capitalization over the past 40 years, you would have trailed the market benchmark by 234bp per annum. At the end of that period, you would have had accumulated more than 2.5x the amount of money through investing in the broader market gauge versus the S&P 100. This outperformance is even more meaningful when you remember that today the S&P 100 represents nearly half the market cap of the broader market gauge.
The lagging returns by the S&P 100 over the last couple of generations can be thought of as an anti-size factor. If the size factor has delivered long-run outperformance, then owning the very largest companies in the U.S. should be expected to lag. The weighted average market capitalization of the S&P 100 today is a whopping $324B.
Over the last several years, the S&P 100 Index has been dragged higher by the tremendous outperformance of the largest companies. Netflix and Amazon have been in the top 2% of all S&P 500 constituents over the past 5 years for cumulative performance. Facebook is in the top decile. Apple despite its world-leading market cap is just outside the top decile. Alphabet investors only doubled their money over the last five years.
These five companies are likely among the top five holdings of many Seeking Alpha readers. The question one should be asking themselves is whether the multi-year outperformance they have experienced is likely to continue. Is the underperformance of the past two months a beginning of a relative correction for these high-flying stocks? Shouldn't we expect stocks with large growth expectations to reprice late in a business cycle as economic growth fades?
Continued long-run outperofrmance by the megacaps would certainly be anomalous historically. The table below shows the average returns of the S&P 100 vs. the S&P 500.
The S&P 500 has outperformed the S&P 100 in 28 of the 41 full years in the dataset, including the first sixteen. Notably, the largest years of outperformance for the S&P 100 were 1998 and 1999 during the height of the tech boom. Nearly 20 years forward, we are seeing tech stalwarts drive the market higher again. At the end of 1999, Microsoft, Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO ), Intel (NASDAQ: INTC ), Alcatel-Lucent ( LU ), and International Business Machines (NYSE: IBM ) were all among the ten largest companies by market capitalization. Oracle ( ORCL ; #11), Nortel (#18), Dell (#20), Java (#22), HP Inc. ( HPQ ; #23), Yahoo ( YHOO ; #24), Qualcomm ( QCOM ; #25), and EMC (#26) were not far behind.
There are many reasons to suggest why this time is different for tech leadership. These companies have become dominant market players in markets that are important to end consumers (mobile devices, email, internet search, social networking, cloud computing, online retail). I am not sold though. Historically, you have not seen the companies with the highest market capitalizations continue to generate market-beating returns over long-time intervals.
This table shows that outperformance by the market giants has been concentrated in the run-up to the tech bubble, the run-up to the Great Recession, and the recent expansion. As prices rise, valuations become stretched as the market prices in strong growth for extended time intervals. I think the bar is now too high, and would expect a broad market benchmark to outperform the largest capitalization companies over forward periods. The past two months may be the start of something bigger for the tech giants.
